clinicalPearls: C5 deficiency is a terminal-pathway defect that markedly predisposes to invasive and recurrent Neisseria infection, particularly meningococcal disease.
Meningococcal infections in terminal-complement deficiency often involve unusual or non-groupable serogroups and may recur.
It is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner and, unlike C3 deficiency, is not associated with severe pyogenic infection or major autoimmune disease.
CH50 and AH50 are both markedly reduced or absent because the terminal lytic pathway is shared, while individual upstream components are normal.
A low or absent C5 antigenic level confirms the diagnosis after terminal-pathway failure is demonstrated.
C5 also generates the potent anaphylatoxin C5a, but the clinical phenotype is dominated by defective membrane attack complex formation.
Meningococcal vaccination, including serogroup B and the quadrivalent conjugate vaccine, is a cornerstone of management.
Any febrile illness warrants urgent assessment and empirical antibiotics because meningococcaemia can progress rapidly.
reference.pathophysiology: C5 is the first component of the terminal complement pathway; once cleaved, C5b nucleates assembly of the C5b-9 membrane attack complex that lyses susceptible organisms, most importantly Neisseria species. In C5 deficiency the membrane attack complex cannot form, so serum bactericidal activity against Neisseria is lost, explaining the striking susceptibility to meningococcal and gonococcal infection. Upstream complement functions such as opsonisation and immune-complex clearance remain intact, which is why pyogenic infection with other encapsulated organisms and lupus-like autoimmunity are not prominent. Loss of C5a generation also blunts a component of chemotaxis, but the dominant clinical consequence is failure of complement-mediated killing of Neisseria.
additionalDifferentials: Other terminal-component deficiencies (C6, C7, C8, C9)
additionalInvestigations: CH50 and AH50, both markedly reduced in terminal-pathway defects
Specific C5 antigenic and functional level
Serum bactericidal activity against Neisseria where available
Genetic testing of the C5 gene
Cultures and PCR during acute infection to identify serogroup
Documentation of meningococcal and other vaccination status
Screening of at-risk relatives once an index case is identified
redFlags: Fever with headache, neck stiffness or a non-blanching rash
Rapidly evolving meningococcaemia or septic shock
Any febrile illness in a known terminal-complement-deficient patient
reference.prognosis: With meningococcal vaccination, patient education and prompt treatment of febrile illness, most individuals do well; the principal risk is recurrent neisserial infection, which although often less fatal than in the general population can still be life-threatening if not treated promptly.
pitfalls: Not testing for terminal-complement deficiency after a first or recurrent meningococcal infection.
Assuming standard childhood immunisation is sufficient without serogroup B and conjugate meningococcal vaccines.
Delaying empirical antibiotics in a febrile deficient patient.
Confusing terminal-pathway deficiency with early-component defects, which have a different phenotype.
Failing to screen and counsel affected family members.
references: Middleton's Allergy: Principles and Practice, current edition
Oxford Textbook of Medicine, current edition
Reviews on terminal complement deficiency and neisserial infection
management: Prioritise meningococcal immunisation with both quadrivalent conjugate (ACWY) and serogroup B vaccines, maintaining boosters, to offset defective membrane-attack-complex killing of Neisseria.
Ensure pneumococcal and Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccines are also kept up to date.
Treat any febrile illness urgently with empirical antibiotics active against Neisseria meningitidis, as invasive disease can recur.
Consider long-term prophylactic penicillin in those with recurrent meningococcal infection.
Educate patient and family to recognise meningococcal symptoms and seek immediate care, with a standby emergency plan.
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance and screen siblings for terminal-complement deficiency.
